reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with postprandial epigastric pain, food-fear-related weight loss, and sometimes an epigastric bruit that varies with respiration
Caused by extrinsic compression of the coeliac axis (and often its neural plexus) by a low-lying median arcuate ligament
Compression is typically worse in expiration, when the coeliac artery is drawn upward against the ligament
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful evaluation for other causes of chronic abdominal pain
Duplex ultrasound with respiratory manoeuvres shows increased coeliac artery velocities that worsen on expiration
Cross-sectional angiography demonstrates the characteristic focal hooked narrowing of the proximal coeliac artery
Definitive treatment is ligament release (often laparoscopic or robotic) to decompress the artery and coeliac plexus
reference.pathophysiology: In median arcuate ligament syndrome, a low-lying or hypertrophied median arcuate ligament (the fibrous arch connecting the diaphragmatic crura) compresses the proximal coeliac artery and the surrounding coeliac neural plexus. The compression is dynamic, tightening during expiration as the artery rides upward. Symptoms are attributed both to a degree of foregut ischaemia or flow limitation and, importantly, to irritation of the compressed coeliac plexus, which may explain the disproportionate, meal-related pain despite generally rich collateral mesenteric circulation.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia from atherosclerotic disease
Functional dyspepsia or other functional gut-brain disorders
additionalInvestigations: Mesenteric duplex ultrasound with inspiratory and expiratory measurements of coeliac velocities
CT or MR angiography to show the hooked coeliac stenosis and exclude other pathology
Upper endoscopy to exclude peptic disease
Cross-sectional abdominal imaging to evaluate pancreas and biliary tree
Coeliac plexus block as a diagnostic and prognostic manoeuvre in selected patients
redFlags: Weight loss and food avoidance raising concern for malignancy or true mesenteric ischaemia
Acute severe abdominal pain suggesting an alternative vascular emergency
Persistent symptoms after other causes have been excluded
Signs of gastrointestinal bleeding pointing to another diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Outcomes after ligament release are variable but often favourable in carefully selected patients, particularly younger patients with classic postprandial pain and confirmed dynamic compression; symptom persistence can occur when the diagnosis is misapplied.
pitfalls: Diagnosing MALS from an incidental coeliac indentation on imaging in an asymptomatic patient
Failing to perform respiratory-phase imaging to demonstrate dynamic compression
Overlooking other treatable causes of chronic abdominal pain before intervention
Attributing all postoperative symptom relief to arterial rather than neural decompression
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
management: Confirm the diagnosis by excluding other causes of chronic abdominal pain before intervention, as it is a diagnosis of exclusion
Surgical division (release) of the median arcuate ligament to decompress the coeliac axis, by laparoscopic, robotic or open approach, as the definitive treatment
Coeliac plexus neurolysis or ganglionectomy at the time of release to address the neurogenic component of the pain
Coeliac artery revascularisation with angioplasty and stenting or bypass grafting where a fixed residual stenosis persists after ligament release
Nutritional support and dietary optimisation to reverse food-fear-related weight loss
Coeliac plexus block as a diagnostic and prognostic step and for symptomatic relief in selected patients
Manage through a multidisciplinary vascular surgery, gastroenterology and pain team, reserving surgery for carefully selected patients
Postoperative duplex surveillance of coeliac flow with monitoring for symptom recurrence
